HEADLINE: Top Ends bottom line looks good
TEXT:
With its good weather, relaxed lifestyle and strong property and rental market, Darwin is an attractive proposition. By SUE WILLIAMS

Darwin used to be the only city in Australia where people preferred to talk about fishing, the footy, the weather, the latest croc story… anything other than property. But no more.

Now, at every dinner party, every bar, and every coffee shop, the stunning rise in prices in Darwin’s housing market is the subject on everyone’s lips.

“Well, it is pretty incredible,” says Chris Clarke of Real Estate Central NT. “And now Darwin seems to have become the most attractive place in Australia.”

He has a point. The city has seen a flood of people from Victoria, NSW, Queensland and South Australia coming to settle in a territory capital that’s been virtually untouched by COVID-19.

It has a balmy climate, a famously relaxed lifestyle and, as Australia’s least populated capital – just 147,231 residents and a density of about 46 people per square kilometre – it has even more post-pandemic charm.

“Darwin is an amazing place to be,” says one of the latest arrivals, radiologist and nuclear medicine specialist Dr John Eng, who’s just moved from Victoria with his family and commutes back every three weeks for work.

“There’s no COVID, it’s tropical and it’s great for kids. There’s also much more space, and housing prices are a lot more affordable than in Melbourne. It’s only a four-hour flight, and you could easily spend four hours in a car to go somewhere, so this is the best of both worlds.”

With demand for property surging, investors are now seeing good growth, excellent returns and minuscule vacancy rates. Over the quarter to the end of March 2021, on Domain Group figures, house prices in Darwin rose by 9.1 per cent, second nationally only to Canberra’s 9.7 per cent. Over the past year, apartment prices rose 20.2 per cent.

Rents are strong too, with the median weekly rent for a three-bedroom house sitting at $505, up 19.5 per cent over the past year, and a twobedroom unit at $400, up 14.3 per cent on 2020. And, of perhaps even more interest to investors, vacancy rates are now the secondlowest – after Hobart – of the capital cities at 0.5 per cent, down 80.9 per cent over the year.

Real Estate Institute of Northern Territory president Quentin Kilian is enthusiastic.

“Everyone should be buying here, particularly investors,” he says. “We consistently have rental yields over 5 per cent, the highest in Australia.

We were the first to open our borders, and the migration north started in June last year.

“We’re seeing so many Victorians, in particular, relocating up here, and why wouldn’t they? It’s 32 degrees outside today.

Property here is so much more affordable ...

you’re getting much more for your money.”

Indeed, the median house price in Darwin is now $554,295, and units $293,731 – both the lowest of all capital cities.

“We’ve had a lot of interstate buyers looking to get away from COVID and wanting a nice climate and a good lifestyle,” says Kerri-Ann Laurence of North Property NT. “I sold a beautiful house the other day for $1.37 million in a good suburb that would cost $6 million to $8 million elsewhere.”

HEADLINE: Living in Bangalow
TEXT:
Bangalow is a can-do community that lives a chilled-out lifestyle close to the beach and the airport. By KATE FARRELLY

On a visit to family in Bangalow 11 years ago, Ben Alcock and his wife Grescha Brewer thought it would be a lovely place to retire to … sometime.

Fast-forward two weeks and the couple were packing up their Sydney home and making the move after a serendipitous job vacancy landed Brewer a job at the local aged-care facility.

“It was a crazy set of circumstances,” Alcock says. “If it hadn’t happened that fast we probably would have talked ourselves out of it. We thought we would give it a year or so and see how it goes, and we’re still here 11 years later, embedded in the community. We’re still pinching ourselves about this little life we’ve created up here.”

Getting involved Perhaps not so little: Alcock has his fingers in many local pies, from a financial technology start-up to a first-rate film festival that premiered at the Bangalow Showground earlier this year and is set to become an annual event.

“Once you open yourself up to the community lots of things swim into view and you can participate as a punter or sometimes get lucky enough to get stuck in as an operator,” he says.

Alcock has worked on ABC North Coast radio, freelances as a writer and content producer and dabbles in pickling, winning blue rosettes at the Bangalow Show off the back of his aunt’s pickled onion recipe.

Away from the crowds of Byron Bay but still close by, Bangalow offers a slower, rural lifestyle in a vibrant community.

For sale Agent: Ed Silk Byron Bay, Ed Silk 0418 660 063 With sweeping district views from its ridgeline position, this contemporary residence with a horizon-edge pool sits on almost 40 hectares, currently home to 3500 macadamia trees and 300 finger lime trees.

Bangalow Byron Bay 18 Pioneers Crescent $16 million 3 5 5 YOU MAY LIKE ...

“When you’re in Sydney and you go to the Royal Easter Show each year, it doesn’t feel personal,” he says. “But when you’re in a small town and they have an annual agricultural show the community gets excited about baking cakes and lamingtons, and the kids are baking shortbreads and doing artworks and entering in pavilion categories. It’s pretty hard not to get caught up in it and it’s super-fun!” Alcock describes the Bangalow community as a creative, entrepreneurial bunch looking for a slightly quieter life. He believes living beyond the city is a great way to buy time to chase dreams.

“It gives you the headspace to look up and look around, which you sometimes miss when you’re on a bus for 45 minutes, looking at your phone.”

So central Alcock loves having Byron Bay close by and also enjoys visiting the surrounding towns of Clunes, Brunswick Heads, Lennox Head and Federal.

Ed Silk Byron Bay principal Ed Silk says the whole region offers so much while also being close to the coast and the airport.

He reports increasing migration from out west, with farmers downsizing to Bangalow, and plenty of interest from Sydney and Melbourne families.

Homes at the top end of the market are tightly held, with homeowners building their dream properties and staying on to “live the dream”.

HEADLINE: For sublime design, start in a good place
TEXT:
Two of Australia’s top architects discuss what it takes to create the best in prestige homes. By SUE WILLIAMS   An excellent location is always important when building, buying or renovating a property, but for prestige home-owners it’s absolutely critical.

While they want to enjoy their precious leisure time as much as they can, they also want to ensure such a major asset grows in value.

“There are a number of fundamental ingredients to deciding on the right location,” says internationally acclaimed architect Rob Mills, who’s designed some of Sydney and Melbourne’s most beautiful homes, as well as many overseas.

“The starting point is proximity to an international airport or within an hour and a quarter’s drive to a major city.

“The next things are a temperate or warmer climate, views of the water and either boating in a safe harbour or a beach, and a good culture.

You need to have quality produce available, great stores, cafes and restaurants.”

Mills’ A-list locations for prestige properties include Portsea on the tip of Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula, Palm Beach on Sydney’s northern beaches and Noosa, the jewel of the Sunshine Coast.

Then, closer in, he favours Point Piper, Darling Point, Elizabeth Bay, Vaucluse, Bellevue Hill and Mosman in Sydney, and, in Melbourne, South Yarra, Toorak, Armadale, Brighton and Hawthorn.

In Brisbane, a favourite is Hamilton, in Perth, Dalkeith and, in Tasmania, anywhere around Hobart’s Civic Square.

Less anticipated tips are Umina on the central coast of NSW, Aireys Inlet on Victoria’s Great Ocean Road and Airlie Beach on Queensland’s Whitsunday coast.

But that’s not to say that the coastline further away from the main cities doesn’t have its special spots too.

One of the things world-renowned architect John Wardle loves most about Australia is that there are so many gorgeous rural landscapes that continue right down to the ocean.

“That means you can have a remarkable retreat on an incredible part of the coast, but you can also have a productive farm,” he says.

“That can be a very valuable antidote to our lives in the cities.

“At the same time, however, I’m always aghast when I see people build ‘city houses’ in the countryside or on the coast.

“You see them in both NSW and Victoria, and they’re really inappropriate buildings and look appalling when you apply a city aesthetic to a very different landscape.”

As well as making sure such houses fit their setting, with the use of the right local stone and timber and sustainable design, and with careful regard to the area’s history, the owners of such houses also have an obligation to make a contribution to the place, and to the community of which they become a part, Wardle believes.

At his own home on Tasmania’s Bruny Island, he planted 10,000 trees and turned a third of the property into a sanctuary, winning the Greening Australia Award for the most sustainable farm in the state.

“That’s something I’m very passionate about,” Wardle says.

His favourite areas for prestige properties are on the south coast and central coast of NSW, on the west coast of Victoria near the Great Ocean Road, around the Margaret River in Western Australia and the coastline of Tasmania, from the wild, rugged land of the west to the agricultural lands of the east coast.

Yet, not everyone chooses to have both a city house and a home in the country or at the coast in these post-pandemic days. Now, many more prestige property owners are choosing to combine the two – or three – Mills says.

Instead of facing the difficulties of travelling between their various homes, especially if any are overseas or interstate, and bearing the expense of capital gains tax, a number are now planning renovations of their existing places of residence to give the houses much more of a resort feel – a peaceful, sensory escape from the hustle bustle of life outside.

For some, that means a series of living spaces to enjoy with family and friends, places to play games and share meals, outdoor living areas, a movie theatre, plenty of garaging for car collections, and wellness centres with a gym, a sauna and a massage space.

“Travel can be difficult these days, and people are time-poor, so they want to make sure they can have the best living experience possible at home,” Mills says.

“As a result, prestige property, now more than ever, requires a triple-A location. It doesn’t make sense to build an exotic house anywhere that’s not quality.”

HEADLINE: Note from the editor
TEXT: One pandemic-induced trend that isn’t going away just yet is our flight from the city. And while some are lucky enough to keep homes in the city and the country, an increasing number of Australians are choosing to move permanently to the country or the coast. So, if that new home is to be permanent, why not start from scratch? In our feature story this week, we speak to two of Australia’s leading architects on how to choose the best spots to build for great views and increasing property values. One area that has well and truly boomed is NSW’s Northern Rivers region, which we’re visiting in Living In this week. Bangalow’s housing market is tightly held, with its residents loving how close it is to Byron Bay but without the crowds. And heading even further north, The Property Investor asks whether it’s a good time to invest in Darwin.

HEADLINE: Fishy Business
TEXT:
Your most recent appointmentwas as culinary director at Pt. Leo Estate on Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula,which has an impressive sculpturepark. It seemsbeingsurroundedby art has rubbedoff onyou?

Itwas one of the key factors as to why I went down there. Having those sculptures constantly in front of you was amazingly inspirational.

Whendidyoustart creatingyour ownart?

I’ve always loved to draw, through school and high school I took art classes, although I was not necessarily doing all the homework. In fact it was the only subject at high schoolwhere my mumgot a phone call fromthe teacherwho said if I don’t start doing the homework I’ll fail. But I always loved it. It’s something I use to distract myself. I use it towind down a little bit.

Have you had much formal training?

Aside from school, the one piece of formal training I’ve had was a life drawing class at Brett Whiteley Studio.You go once a week and you stand in his studio at Surry Hills surrounded by his work. You’ll do your 10-second, five-second, five-minute drawings with the teacher and in between you get a chance to wander around. There are a lot of Whiteley’s charcoal works on the walls and you can look at his line and the way he created. He left all of his workings on the page.You can see howhe’d changed his drawings, you can see his process.And that’s part of the joy of his work.

What do you draw?

I do like to draw faces and people. I don’t knowif I’m that good at it. I went through a period of drawing flowers and of trying to draw hands, which are incredibly difficult. I draw with pens and also charcoal. I also use pencil and go over it with pastel.

Doyoudo landscapes?

No, but I often drawoverlooking thewater.

InVictoriawe had a great place overlooking Port Phillip Bay so I’d often be drawingwith the water as a backdrop. I love drawing in the open so that you can be really absorbed by what you’re doing.

What’s your thinking about the idea of food as a form of art?

I oscillate a little bit. Being a cook or a chef is very technical and it’s almost like science in a lot ofways. But there’s also freedomof expression, especially in fine dining. So you often find chefs use art as part of the practice. Alain Passard does wonderful collages. When I was an apprentice, before cameras on phones were a thing, I had a journal and after I went out to dinner I would go home and drawall the dishes I’d had so I could remember how they looked on the plate. I still have the journal.

Even now I find that desserts are useful to draw. They’re technical and they take a lot more towork out. Savoury is immediate, dessert takes structure and form. Dessert is closest you get to an artwork in cuisine.

Howdo you feelwhen people photograph your food?

It’s great.Go for it. I like to seewhat people focus on. It can inform you onwhat’s working, what’s not working.

Yournewrestaurantwill open inPaddington, Sydneyinspring.Will therebeanyPhilWoods on thewalls?

No, not on the walls. At home I do have one work that’s framed and on display. It’s from one of theWhiteley life-drawing sessions.

It’s of an older model, she had a red handkerchief tied through her hair. Shewas fun to draw. I drew it on a daywhen the teacher had told us to draw with our non-dominant hand. It was really hard, and I’m really dominant right hand. When you’re dominant on one hand your mind controls what you’re doing and often your lines become static, a little bit contrived.

When you use your non-dominant hand, yourmind doesn’t have as much control over what it’s doing and your drawing becomes more expressive and free. It’s amazing. •

HEADLINE: Fishy Business
TEXT:
JULY AFRMAGAZINE 41 Whyhasn’t the internetkilledthe cookbook?

Poring. You can browse recipes on the internet all day (I certainly do), and if you knowwhat you’re looking for, the power of search yields much treasure, especially for culinary cultures that hadn’t seen much interest fromtraditional publishers in English. But themechanics of it are just not as pleasurable as leafing through a real book.Also, there’s a lot of really terrible recipes to wade through online before you get to the good stuff.

Are cookbooks the newadventure books?

There’s certainlymore adventure in them than there used to be.Death, divorce, social justice, history, ecology. I think publishers are starting to understand the potential for food in its centrality in everyday life but also its more profound implications at a macro level. Food is the single biggest contributor to climate change, and that problemappears to beworsening rather than improving.

What are youreadingnow?

Gringos by Charles Portis; Nyernila, a book ofAboriginal creation stories of Victoria; and John Lanchester on shipping in the 22nd April issue of the London Review of Books. Not much food there, with the exception of a mouth-watering Boon Wurrung story in Nyernila about trapping fat eels and smoking themover coals.

Who is your favouritefoodwriter?

I have a lot of time for Patience Gray; she lived a very interesting life and her book Honey From aWeed brims with the richness of her experience.

Cookbooks of the moment?

Always Add Lemon and Parwana are top ofmind; both Danielle Alvarez and Durkhanai Ayubi will expand your culinary horizons, and I’m forward to talking snacks with them atMFWF this winter.

A favouriteboozebook?

Kingsley Amis’ Everyday Drinking is pleasingly opinionated, and the hangover scene in Lucky Jim is in a class of its own.

For the hideousness of boozing gonewrong, BloodMeridian by CormacMcCarthy is hard to beat.Meanwhile,Max Allen’s Intoxicating will almost certainly broaden the way you think about drink inAustralia.

Thoughheopenswithanaphorismcoinedby the 18th-century anti-slavery activistWilliamFox calling foraboycottonWest Indiansugar andrum – “Ifwepurchasethe commodity, weparticipate inthe crime” – it’s not just the salmon consumers at the tablewho should readToxic. This is a shockingstoryonmany fronts, about corporate greed, regulatory failure, the destruction of ecosystems and erosion of public trust. It’s even moreshockingbecause thewhole sorry storyhas beenhidinginplain sight for 30years. Itmightbe Flanagan’smost importantwork yet.

The Tasmanian author skewers the largely successfulmarketing spinbyBigSalmon(as he labels the island’s biggest salmon companies) about the supposed health benefits of eating farmed salmon, sustainability, efficiency and world’s best practice. In the process he investigates the shadowy provenance of fish food: fish meal, oil and soy sourced in South America and linked to deforestation, chicken guts, ethoxyquin,which is a petrochemical stabiliser banned in food for humans, and a synthetic dye responsible for thepink colour of farmed salmon.

Hedescribes thecruelty anddisease rife in the “gigantic floating feedlots” of fish farms and outlines the increasingly costlymeasures needed to keep “thewrong species in thewrong environment”. Thesemeasures include “seal bombing” long-nosed fur seals to keep them away fromfish pens, and the drawing and dumpingof huge supplies of contaminated fresh water used to “bathe” salmonofgill amoeba.

“The cost of keeping so many salmon alive in circumstances inwhichtheywouldotherwisebe dead is the destruction of the surrounding marine ecosystem,” Flanaganwrites, and thetally is chilling. The impact of vast volumes of fish waste includes “death zones” beneathfeedlots,massive algal and jellyfish blooms, and the devastation of native flora and fauna.

None of this should be surprising. A 2016 ABC Four Corners investigation revealedwidespread READING MATTERS PAT NOURSE  SECOND PLACE RACHEL CUSK / FABER FICTION Canadian-born and Britishbased writer Rachel Cusk has written 10highly regarded novels, and three searingly honestworks of non-fiction focusedonmotherhood, marriageanddivorce. Inher later novels, a chief preoccupation is findinganarrativeformthat eschews the conventions of realist fiction – character, she believes, is dead – for something closer to lived experience.

Her latest novel, SecondPlace, is loosely based onAmerican socialiteMabelDodgeLuhan’s memoir, Lorenzo inTaos,ofD.H. Lawrence’sstay withher inNewMexico. It iswrittenintheformof lettersexchangedbetweenawomanknownbyher initialM(presumablyMabel) and a certain Jeffers (a nod to the American poetRobinson Jefferswho wasatTaos), centredonher invitationtoanartist,L (Lawrence),whocomes tovisitherandherhusband at their “secondplace”–“ahomefor…thehigher things…I neededsomedegree of communication, however small,withthenotionsof artandwiththe peoplewhoabide by these notions.”

The story framesmoral and psychological quandaries as aesthetic questions – questions about art. The result is an important novel of quiet profundity but little levity. “I liked fun andwanted to have it,”Mclaims early in the novel. Later, though, sheconfesses toL: “I’venever had enoughfun.” It’s a tellingremark.• destruction causedby intensivesalmonfarming inMacquarieHarbour, closetoaWorldHeritage areaonthewest coastofTasmania.Worsestill, theTasmaniansalmonindustry is set todouble in sizeby 2030, Flanagan claims,evenasocean farming is being rapidly eclipsed around theworld by more sustainable land-based salmon farms.

Themost impassionedpassages inToxic describe the human costs of salmon farming in Tasmania. Drawingonextensive interviewswith scientists,whistleblowers and residents, Flanagan describes peaceofminddestroyedby relentless noise, filth and light pollution, and growing distress aswaterways arefouledandmarine life disappears. He levels claims of evasionand lies fromindustry, politicians and bureaucratswhen communities and individuals – including him – complain. For 15 years he says hehaswitnessed the slowdestructionof thewaterwaynear his shackonBruny Island, “our family’s heart-place”.

His criticismof industry and successive state governments is scathing. And yet, hewrites, “the problem,finally, wasn’t theindustryor the government, but us. Itwaswe Tasmanians…who thought thatwe couldtrashour seas, likewehad somanyother things, and somehowtherewould benoimpact ... Itwaswewho stayed silent for too long.” Silent nomore.

HEADLINE: A surfeit of greens
TEXT:
While nothing can replace good lines, the colour of a watch face is a delightful diversion

CANYOUHAVETOOMANY greens? Not if you’re supping at the bountiful table of timekeeping, where it seems a brandwithout a greendialled watch is a brand not worth accommodating on your wrist.

This, afterwe’ve managed to rack up five centuries of watchmakingwithout the need for such a hue – and cry. The culprit is possibly that muscular interloper Panerai, which a decade back introduced a model designated the PAM 382, better known as the Bronzo because itwas cased in bronze and featured a green dial. Limited to 1000 pieces, it was a hefty hit with watchy types, something that didn’t go unnoticed by competitors. Itwould have been reasonable to credit the bronze casing alone for its allure, given this material hadn’t been seen on a watch since no one could remember.

And indeed, thanks to Panerai, we now have a plethora of bronze-cased watches.

But the green dial,where did that come from? Research?You can picture the scene.

All is calm in the pin-drop valleys of Swiss watchmaking when a white-coated technician, clipboard in hand, bursts into the boardroom: “Jean-Claude, Jean Claude, we’ve found themissing link – and it’s green.”Kind of puts into perspective inventor George Daniels and his co-axial movement – another breakthrough, but alas, with nothing like the go of a good green, it was embraced by only one brand,Omega.

These days I’mthe victimof “greenmail” on an almost daily basis, alertingme to fresh arrivals flaunting green face-paint, some more successful than others. This shouldn’t surprise given there’s a wider range of greens than formost colours – bottle, lime, emerald, pea, sea, sage, acid, fluoro, khaki and eau de nil.

Predictably the Swiss have mostly gone for the darker tints, the exception being Breitling chief executive Georges Kern, who’s choice for the brand’s Premier B09 Heritagemodel suggests – time will tell – colour-blindness or genius. Not for him a shade indistinguishable fromblack, but the startling pop of pistachio.Whether that appeals to you or not, it’sworth seeing in person – and safe to say it’s never been seen on a watch before.

Greenish full-lume dials are also proving popular, the latest to ping intomy inbox is a collaboration fromBulgari and apparent DJ Steve Aoki who the email asserts, is a “true visionary with 3 billion music streams to his name”.Obviously, then, the entertainer-producer-artist is a 21stcentury natural for a watch huddle.

Consequently, his signature appears on the glowing green dial of a special edition of the brand’s aluminiumwatch, one that “brings together the essence of values driving both partners” and is “dedicated to lovers of life, optimism andmovement”.

Praise be the Lord and let’s hope it works for a timepiece thatmight need a little help.

This diversion aside, themost attractive newcomers derive their luminosity from design as much as colouration, their new coat of green merely highlighting lines that already flatter thewrist.As towhich is the most desirable, it depends primarily on your brand preference andmonetary resilience, although a blind tasting might suggest some surprise winners.

The green garb gives Longines’ Spirit model a buffedmilitary appeal, while for Cartier an almost British racing green brings an entry-level Tank to life, the dial unencumbered by anything as pedestrian as numerals or other markings. It works a treat.At Jaeger-LeCoultre, it’s this year’s Reverso Tribute Small Seconds that gets a slightly deeper greenmakeover,while Tag Heuer has dipped twice into the pot,with a sunray green for the iconicMonaco and a teal green for a Carrera limited-edition based on the 1963 original.

These are hardly unfamiliar watches; their profiles have beenwith us for yonks, but somehowthey’re looking as fresh as the upgraded internals that power them. The Carrera, in particular, looks more handsome than ever, benefitting from a sizing of 39mm– not too small, not too big.

Given there are only 500, it mightn’t even be a bad investment, although in that category itwould be hard to beat Patek’s olivecheekedNautilus, nor Panerai’s Bronzo, which has tripled its retail ask as years have passed. But if it’s simply a coloured dial you’re looking for, well, this is your year, never mind about the green folding stuff. • BaniMcSpedden iswatcheditorof The Australian Financial Review.
